title: Recursion & Backtracking
relevance: High | Foundational for nearly all OA graph/matrix pathfinding and combination generation.
company_notes: Word Search–style string pathfinding on 2D grids with obstacles (Amazon/Microsoft). Distributing items into K buckets / equal partitions (Matchsticks to Square style). Valid combinations under an exact budget without duplicates (Capital One). OAs with N ≤ 20 or N ≤ 15 that look like DP but are pruned backtracking.

phases.goal: Establish when the candidate recognizes backtracking from tiny N, generate-all wording, or small-matrix path search.

must_hit.point: Extremely small constraints like N ≤ 20 signal exploring all states via recursion/backtracking rather than heavy DP.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Points at N ≤ 20 (or similarly tiny N) as the cue for a searchable state tree.

must_hit.point: Keywords like "find all valid combinations", "generate", or "how many ways" without a modulo mark combination/permutation generation.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Names generate-all / combinations / ways-without-modulo as the trigger.

must_hit.point: Searching for an explicit path on a small matrix (Word Search–style) is classic 2D grid DFS backtracking.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Maps path-on-grid wording to matrix DFS with undo.

must_hit.point: An OA with N ≤ 20 or N ≤ 15 that looks like DP is often a simple backtracking tree with pruning, not DP.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Says don't default to DP; try pruned exhaustive search under those bounds.

probes: What in the statement makes you reach for backtracking instead of DP or greedy?
When do tiny N and "generate all" / path-on-grid cues point to recursion with undo?

hints.1: Look at constraint size and whether the ask is generate-all, count ways, or find a path.
hints.2: N ≤ 20 plus combinations/generate/ways-without-modulo, or a small matrix path, usually means build-and-abandon search.
hints.3: Say: N ≤ 20 / N ≤ 15 → searchable tree; "generate"/combinations/ways → backtracking; small-grid path → DFS with undo; don't assume DP.

phases.goal: Get the candidate to state incremental candidate building, abandon-on-invalid, and the main generation templates before coding.

must_hit.point: Explore subsets, permutations, or paths by building a candidate incrementally and abandoning it the moment it cannot yield a valid solution.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States build-then-backtrack / prune-invalid as the core idea.

must_hit.point: Subsets use take-it-or-leave-it recursion; size-K combinations and Combination Sum add reuse or start-index constraints in the tree.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Describes include/exclude subsets and start-index / reuse rules for combinations.

must_hit.point: Permutations are the O(N!) generation template; constrained generation (e.g. Generate Parentheses) prunes with state parameters like open vs closed counts.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Names O(N!) perms and parameter-based pruning for invalid branches.

must_hit.point: Prune early when a branch exceeds limits (e.g. sum > target) or sort largest-first (Matchsticks to Square) so bad partitions fail faster.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Mentions sum>target cutoffs and descending sort for K-partition pruning.

probes: How do you describe the backtracking loop before you write code?
Which template do you pick for subsets vs permutations vs constrained generation, and where do you prune?

hints.1: Think in terms of growing a partial answer and undoing when it breaks.
hints.2: Separate take-it-or-leave-it subsets, O(N!) perms, and state-parameter pruning.
hints.3: Say: build candidate, abandon when invalid; subsets include/exclude; perms O(N!); prune with open/closed or sum>target; largest-first for Matchsticks.

phases.goal: Confirm the candidate can write the standard subset, permutation, duplicate-skip, partition, grid, and N-Queens templates from memory.

must_hit.point: Write clean take-it-or-leave-it subset generation; optionally map masks from 0 to 2^N-1 as an iterative subset alternate.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Sketches include/exclude recursion and/or loop masks 0..2^N-1.

must_hit.point: Write O(N!) permutations both via swap-based logic and via a boolean visited array.
Skip duplicates after sorting with if (i > start && nums[i] == nums[i-1]) continue; for subsets/permutations/combination-sum variants.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States sort plus that adjacent-equal skip idiom.

must_hit.point: String partitioning: iterate cut lengths and recurse on suffixes; 2D grid DFS marks visited or sets board[i][j] = '*' then undoes; N-Queens diagonals use row + col and row - col + n - 1 for O(1) checks.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Mentions suffix recursion, grid mark/undo, and those two diagonal index formulas.

probes: Write the subset include/exclude skeleton and the duplicate-skip line after sorting.
How do you implement permutations (swap vs visited), grid mark/undo, and O(1) N-Queens diagonal checks?

hints.1: Start from the subset template, then layer perms and undo.
hints.2: Add the sort + adjacent skip; for grids mark then restore; for queens track diagonals in arrays.
hints.3: Say: include/exclude or masks 0..2^N-1; swap or visited for O(N!); if (i > start && nums[i] == nums[i-1]) continue; suffix cuts; board[i][j]='*' undo; diagonals row+col and row-col+n-1.

phases.goal: State the exponential regimes that make these templates feasible only under tiny N.

must_hit.point: Full permutation generation is O(N!); it is a building-block cost, not something you run for large N.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Quotes O(N!) for the permutations template.

must_hit.point: Subset enumeration via recursion or masks over 0..2^N-1 is feasible when N ≤ 20 (or similarly N ≤ 15 in OAs).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Ties 2^N-style subset search to N ≤ 20 / N ≤ 15.

must_hit.point: N-Queens diagonal tracking arrays give O(1) validity checks per placement attempt instead of scanning the board.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States O(1) diagonal checks via the linear index arrays.

probes: What complexity do you quote for permutations versus full subset enumeration?
Why do N ≤ 20 constraints make 2^N-style search acceptable, and what does O(1) diagonal tracking buy you?

hints.1: Separate permutation blow-up from subset 2^N search.
hints.2: O(N!) for perms; masks/subsets when N ≤ 20; queens want O(1) diagonal tests.
hints.3: Say: perms O(N!); subsets/masks 0..2^N-1 under N ≤ 20 or N ≤ 15; diagonals row+col / row-col+n-1 → O(1) checks.

phases.goal: Surface mislabeling as DP, missing undo, broken duplicate skipping, and weak pruning.

must_hit.point: Seeing N ≤ 20 or N ≤ 15 and defaulting to DP when a pruned backtracking tree is enough.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Corrects the DP reflex and names simple backtracking with pruning.

must_hit.point: Generating subsets/permutations with duplicates without sorting and skipping adjacent equals via if (i > start && nums[i] == nums[i-1]) continue;.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States sort + that continue guard as the fix.

must_hit.point: Forgetting to undo grid marks (visited / board[i][j] = '*') or other candidate state after returning from a recursive call.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Emphasizes restore-after-recurse as the "back" in backtracking.

must_hit.point: Continuing branches that already exceed limits (e.g. sum > target) instead of pruning, or skipping largest-first ordering on K-partition problems like Matchsticks to Square.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Mentions early terminate on over-limit and descending sort to fail faster.

probes: What goes wrong if you treat a tiny-N generate-all OA as DP?
Where do people forget undo, duplicate skipping, or early pruning in these templates?

hints.1: Ask whether you restored state and whether duplicates were filtered.
hints.2: N ≤ 20 ≠ automatic DP; sort+skip duplicates; undo marks; prune sum>target.
hints.3: List: backtracking not DP under N ≤ 20/15; use the adjacent-equal continue; restore visited/'*'; prune over-limit / sort descending for Matchsticks.

tradeoffs.topic: Recursive take-it-or-leave-it subsets vs iterative masks from 0 to 2^N-1
tradeoffs.strong_answer: The recursive include/exclude template is the standard interview form; mapping 0..2^N-1 to binary choices is an alternate iterative way to generate the same power set under tiny N.

tradeoffs.topic: Swap-based permutations vs boolean visited array
tradeoffs.strong_answer: Both realize O(N!) generation: swap-based rearranges in place; a visited array builds the permutation by choosing unused indices—same completeness, different bookkeeping.

tradeoffs.topic: Visited array vs in-place board[i][j] = '*' for grid DFS
tradeoffs.strong_answer: Either marks a cell as used for Word Search–style paths; in-place '*' avoids extra memory but must be undone on backtrack exactly like a visited flag.

tradeoffs.topic: Backtracking with pruning vs assuming DP at N ≤ 20 / N ≤ 15
tradeoffs.strong_answer: Those bounds often mean a searchable tree with pruning (sum limits, state parameters), not that the problem requires DP formulation.

gotchas.trap: Treating an OA with N ≤ 20 or N ≤ 15 as DP by default.
gotchas.correction: It is often a simple backtracking tree with pruning logic, not DP.

gotchas.trap: Emitting duplicate subsets/permutations when the input has duplicate values.
gotchas.correction: Sort the array and skip with if (i > start && nums[i] == nums[i-1]) continue;.

gotchas.trap: Leaving a grid cell marked after a DFS path fails.
gotchas.correction: Undo visited or restore board[i][j] after the recursive call returns.

gotchas.trap: Letting branches run after they already cannot succeed.
gotchas.correction: Terminate when sum > target (or similar limits); for Matchsticks-style K-partition, sorting largest-first fails bad assignments faster.

gotchas.trap: Checking N-Queens diagonals by scanning the board each time.
gotchas.correction: Track diagonals in arrays indexed by row + col and row - col + n - 1 for O(1) validity checks.
